title: Man invested $45M in a Nicolas Cage movie. It got stolen off Netflix’s desk.
gist: Financier Simon Afram and Op-Fortitude sued Netflix after an unencrypted screener drive holding the unreleased Nicolas Cage film Fortitude was stolen from a Netflix office desk and the company allegedly waited about a week to say so. Plaintiffs want at least 2.5x the production budget, or $112.5 million, while Netflix says the production company chose not to encrypt the drive, that no leak has surfaced, and that a $165 million demand amounts to extortion.

insights.claim: Netflix admitted that an unencrypted drive containing the unreleased 2026 film Fortitude was stolen from an office desk along with other drives, and only disclosed it after the production company pressed repeatedly for the screener's return.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Physical media handling remains a live failure point at the largest streaming buyer, despite an industry that markets itself on content security.
insights.quote: Someone stole a good amount of drives from our office desks this past week,

insights.claim: The complaint alleges Netflix knew about the theft for days or a full week before notifying the production company, delaying any response to the risk that the film would leak online.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Notification delay is the fact most likely to drive punitive exposure, independent of who was responsible for encryption.
insights.locator: Netflix had known about the theft

insights.claim: Netflix's own delivery instructions allegedly told the production company to deliver the screener unlocked so it could test the content for a streamlined screening, meaning the drive stayed unencrypted for its entire time in Netflix's possession.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: If proven, this undercuts Netflix's core defense that the filmmaker unilaterally skipped industry-standard safeguards.
insights.quote: This timing allows us to test the content and ensure a streamlined screening,

insights.claim: Netflix's director of Netflix Original Film allegedly claimed thieves would need a key to unlock the movie, an assertion the complaint calls erroneous given Netflix had asked for the drive to be delivered unlocked, and offered only to pay for the missing drive.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: An incorrect internal assurance about encryption status is the kind of contemporaneous record that decides negligence cases.
insights.locator: Rather than acknowledge the profound and devastating loss

insights.claim: The complaint lists the specific controls Netflix allegedly skipped: locked or secured storage, camera-monitored locations, an assigned staff member responsible for the drive, and any tracked chain of custody.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This is effectively a checklist of the minimum custody controls rights-holders should now contract for before handing over any physical asset.
insights.locator: Netflix left the [drive]—which Netflix knew to be unencrypted

insights.claim: Plaintiffs argue that the theft of multiple drives from Netflix desks is itself proof of negligence, regardless of Netflix's claim that the other drives were empty.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Framing the incident as a systemic office-security lapse rather than a single unlucky drive is the plaintiffs' path to punitive damages.
insights.quote: Netflix easily could have, and should have, prevented this precise outcome by taking even a modicum of care and security measures,
insights.locator: Although Netflix claimed the other stolen drives were empty

insights.claim: Op-Fortitude and Simon Afram asked the court to award revenues of at least 2.5 times the production budget, or $112,500,000, plus punitive damages, for an implicit breach of a contract to delete screener files and promptly return the drive.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A 2.5x-budget revenue multiple is the plaintiffs' proposed yardstick for valuing lost first-market exclusivity — a template other rights-holders could copy.
insights.quote: revenues of at least 2.5 times the production budget, or $112,500,000,
insights.locator: They’ve asked the court to rule that Netflix owes them

insights.claim: Netflix denies liability for losing the drive, ruining the marketing strategy or easing piracy, and alleges the plaintiffs are using the suit to extort money after issuing a $165 million demand letter.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The gap between the $165 million demand and the $112.5 million pleaded claim is itself the negotiating range this dispute will settle within.
insights.quote: given their hostile attempts to extort money from Netflix over this situation—including immediately demanding $165 million for the film rather than work with us in good faith.
insights.locator: In response to the lawsuit, Netflix insists

insights.claim: Netflix's public position is that it does not bear the risk of loss for a film delivered without proper industry-standard safeguards, placing responsibility for encryption squarely on the production company.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Risk-of-loss allocation for unencrypted screeners is the legal question this case will settle for the wider acquisition market.
insights.quote: Netflix disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards,
insights.locator: Netflix disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss

insights.claim: Netflix says none of the other stolen drives contained content, that Fortitude was accessible only because the production company did not encrypt it, that the stolen copy is not the only copy, and that there is no evidence of a leak so far.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Absent an actual leak, plaintiffs must prove damages from exposure risk alone, which is a materially harder case.
insights.locator: In a statement to Ars, a Netflix spokesperson confirmed

insights.claim: Netflix says it does not own the rights to Fortitude but has conducted an investigation and offered to monitor known piracy sites for unauthorized distribution or sale of the film.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Piracy-site monitoring is the remedy Netflix considers proportionate — a benchmark for what studios can expect from a buyer after a custody failure.
insights.locator: While we do not own the rights to Fortitude

insights.claim: Afram alleges Netflix refused to provide any information about the nature, scope, status or results of its investigation or security efforts to recover the stolen drive.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Information asymmetry after an incident is itself becoming a litigable harm, relevant to any custodian of third-party assets.

insights.claim: Plaintiffs cannot confirm whether a police report was ever filed and call it telling that Netflix declined their request to involve the Los Angeles Police Department in its internal investigation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Whether a police report exists is a binary discoverable fact that could swing the negligence narrative decisively.
insights.locator: Afram’s team can’t even confirm if a police report was ever filed

insights.claim: The complaint argues Netflix has an incentive to suppress disclosure because acknowledging the theft would also expose its lack of adequate security protocols and the failure of its investigation to recover the drive or identify the thief.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The alleged motive-to-conceal framing is what turns a contract dispute into a punitive-damages claim.
insights.locator: Disclosing the theft and compromise of the Film’s unreleased

insights.claim: Netflix says it stopped coordinating with Afram's legal team only after the money demand was made, while plaintiffs characterize the same silence as hiding evidence to cover its tracks.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Both sides are building a bad-faith record early, which usually signals a long, expensive litigation rather than quick settlement.
insights.locator: Netflix claims that it stopped coordinating

themes.theme: The asset and its scarcity value

insights.claim: Simon Afram personally invested $45 million over seven years to produce Fortitude, a World War II spy story directed by Simon West starring Nicolas Cage and Sir Ben Kingsley, shot on 35-millimeter celluloid.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A single financier carrying full production risk with no studio backstop is exactly the profile most exposed to a custody failure at a buyer.
insights.locator: Afram was so passionate about telling the story

insights.claim: The film's commercial strategy depended on absolute pre-release scarcity: worldwide rights were unsold and no agency had seen it, which is what Afram was marketing when he approached Netflix in mid-June.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Exclusivity is the priced asset in a rights auction, so a security breach destroys value even without an actual leak.
insights.quote: NOBODY has seen it yet, including any of the agencies, and worldwide rights are available,
insights.locator: With a cut of the movie finally available to preview

insights.claim: Netflix responded enthusiastically the same day it received the offer and was shown the film first, before any agency, making it the sole holder of the only screener at the moment of the theft.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Granting an exclusive first look concentrates custody risk in one counterparty — an argument for staggered or controlled screening rooms instead.
insights.locator: This offer was so enticing that it generated an enthusiastic response

insights.claim: Afram says he continues to see tremendous interest in Fortitude and that worldwide rights remain available, indicating the theft has not yet destroyed the sale process.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: If the film still sells at a normal price, the claimed $112.5 million in lost revenue becomes much harder to substantiate.
